bet: one-layer benchmark picks the decoder engine
change: raced a hand-written metal kernel on raw bf16 weights against mpsgraph in 32-bit and accelerate on the cpu, at decoder sizes
result: metal bf16 kernel: 37 ms per step for the 28 layers at 3 rows (79 gb/s). mpsgraph 32-bit: 53 gb/s at 3 rows but 2.5 tflops at 512 rows. cpu sgemm: about 7 steps per second.
why: the bandwidth kernel wins the step, where memory is the limit. apple's kernel wins when many rows share a call.

bet: several rows per thread share a weight read
change: kernels that compute 3, 6, 12 or 24 rows in one thread
result: slower than one thread per value at every width: 12 rows took 71 ms against 47 ms.
why: neighbouring threads already share the weight row through the gpu's caches, and more running sums per thread cost more than they save.

bet: full 32-bit path first
change: encoder, prefill and step on the bandwidth kernel, 32-bit math and cache, batched beams with a slot ancestry table
result: golden test passed on the first complete run. long clip 2.4x realtime: encoder 5.0 s, prefill 14.3 s, 10.7 steps per second.
why: correct first, so later speed work is separated from logic bugs.

bet: apple's matrix kernel for many-row multiplies
change: from 32 rows up, widen the bf16 weights to 32-bit on the fly and call MPSMatrixMultiplication. below that, keep the bandwidth kernel.
result: long clip encoder 5.0 s to 0.8 s, prefill 14.3 s to 3.0 s. tokens and candidates unchanged.
why: 2.7 tflops against about 0.4 for the bandwidth kernel at 1,600 rows. the 32-bit copy is transient, one matrix at a time.

bet: profile by leaving kernels out
change: skip one kernel class per run and compare step times
result: numbers made no sense: skipped kernels leave garbage that changes how long the others run.
why: replaced by a profile mode that gives each kernel its own command buffer and reads the gpu's clock.

bet: no single thread walks a whole row
change: rms norm, softmax and the value mix each looped in one thread. split them into runs of 64 that many threads add in a fixed order.
result: gpu time per step at a 1,700-token context: 166 ms to 70 ms. rms norm 21 ms to 1.4 ms, softmax 18 ms to 1.8 ms, mix 25 ms to 5 ms.
why: serial loops are slow on a gpu. the fixed order keeps a row bit-identical at any batch width.

bet: two running sums in the bandwidth kernel
change: split the dot product into two accumulators
result: interleaved microbenchmark, best of 6: 3 rows 52.9 to 50.5 ms, 6 rows 85.1 to 73.8 ms, 12 rows 148.7 to 145.6 ms. four accumulators were no better.
why: a shorter add chain. the gain is small because the step is near the memory limit.

bet: one thread per weight row for all batch rows
change: read each weight row once and loop over the batch inside the thread
result: 2.7x slower at every width.
why: the long serial loop costs far more than the repeated reads it saves.

bet: encoder on the neural engine
change: a core ml model written from swift, one fixed 8-second window, 16-bit, all 612 operations planned on the neural engine
result: 17 ms per window, 0.27 s for two minutes against 0.8 s on the gpu. same tokens and candidates on the short and medium clips, but it uses 44x and 35x the safety margin.
why: it fails the exactness bar, and the encoder is under 5% of the job. the code stays as an explicit pin outside the exactness claim.

bet: the first long clip was inside 32-bit noise
change: one comparison at step 76 had a gap of 0.00011. transformers' own 32-bit run was 0.90 of the margin away from its 64-bit run there, and the engine was closer to the 64-bit run than the reference was.
result: screened 12 cuts of the same recording for their smallest gap and took the widest, 35.0 to 151.5 s, gap 0.0032. clips are now rejected at half the margin instead of all of it.
why: the plan rejects clips whose closest comparison sits inside 32-bit noise. the test was not loosened.

bet: threads that share a weight row sit side by side
change: swap the grid so the batch runs along a threadgroup and weight rows along the other axis
result: equal at 3 rows, 1.7x slower at 6, 12 and 24 rows.
why: the gpu already reuses the weight row across neighbouring dispatch rows, and the swapped layout breaks up the sequential read.

bet: a wider batch than 12 rows
change: 12 medium clips at once with the batch allowed 12, 24 and 36 rows, interleaved twice
result: 12 rows: 6.95x and 6.26x realtime. 24 rows: 6.09x and 4.10x. 36 rows: 5.65x and 5.59x.
why: past about 12 rows the step is bound by gpu arithmetic, not memory, so wider batches only add cache traffic. 12 stays the default.

bet: how much a wide batch buys
change: three long clips at once with the batch allowed 3, 6 and 9 rows
result: 4.50x, 5.31x and 6.05x realtime, and 4.37x on the repeat at 3 rows. twelve medium clips: 6.0x at 3 rows, 7.7x at 6.
why: sharing weight reads is worth about 1.3x to 1.4x on this mac. the plan's 12 to 20x estimate assumed memory was the only limit, and gpu arithmetic becomes the limit first.

bet: prefill attention on the matrix kernel
change: for a prefill of 64 rows or more, compute scores and the value mix as whole-square matrix products per head on apple's kernel, with the causal mask applied as zero weights in between
result: long clip prefill 3.11 s to 2.25 s (gpu time 4.1 s to 2.2 s in the profile, attention 1.5 s to 0.38 s). tokens and candidates unchanged, margin used 0.05.
why: the per-slot kernels were about 6x below the matrix kernel's arithmetic rate at 1,500 rows.

bet: bandwidth kernel for short prompts
change: prefill of 66 and 164 rows with the matrix kernel switched off, interleaved twice, median of 7
result: 66 rows: 236 and 238 ms with the matrix kernel, 473 and 473 ms without. 164 rows: 327 and 332 ms against 1,177 and 1,215 ms.
why: the matrix kernel wins from a few dozen rows up, even though widening the weights costs about 88 ms per prefill.

bet: a cheaper live draft pass
change: looked for reuse between draft passes of one phrase: cached encoder blocks and a cached audio prefix in the decoder
result: not built. a draft pass costs about 60 ms to encode, 236 ms to prefill and 45 ms per new token. encoder attention spans 8-second windows and the mel floor moves with the loudest frame, so only whole finished windows could be reused, and most phrases are shorter than one window.
why: the reuse only helps phrases longer than 8 s. the per-pass floor is the 88 ms weight widening plus memory-bound steps, so the first draft stays near 0.7 to 1.1 s.

bet: three rows per thread share each weight read
change: a second bandwidth kernel computes three batch rows per thread, each with its own two running sums in the same order as the one-row kernel. used for every decoder matrix and the output head.
result: bit-identical to the one-row kernel at every width. microbenchmark, interleaved best of 6: 3 rows 42.5 to 42.7 ms, 6 rows 54.6 to 43.9, 12 rows 103.4 to 50.7, 24 rows 202.5 to 90.2. twelve medium clips at 12 rows: 6.95x to 12.4x realtime. three long clips at 9 rows: 6.05x to 8.6x.
why: at wide batches each weight row was being read once per batch row. an earlier try at this used arrays of accumulators and lost; with every accumulator in a register it wins.

bet: a batch wider than 12 rows, again
change: with the three-row kernel, twelve medium clips with the batch allowed 12, 24 and 36 rows, interleaved twice
result: 12 rows: 12.4x and 11.9x realtime. 24 rows: 10.0x and 9.7x. 36 rows: 9.9x and 9.3x.
why: past 12 rows a step costs almost as much per row, and each new piece still has to be read in alone between steps. 12 stays the cap.

bet: live text grows token by token
change: a draft pass hands each decoded token to the live session as it comes, and the draft on screen grows from them. a partial that is not yet longer than what is shown changes nothing, so corrections to earlier words still land when the pass ends.
result: golden clips played in at real speed, before, after, before, after on a busy machine. short: 6 updates to 14 and 17, median gap between updates 714 ms to 67 and 52 ms, first text 0.93 s to 0.76 s. medium: 18 updates to 37 and 42, median gap 647 ms to 61 and 50 ms, first text 0.87 s to 0.80 and 0.77 s. settled text was never taken back.
why: the screen used to change only when a whole pass ended. the wait between passes, about 0.5 to 0.9 s to encode, prefill and re-decode the unsettled tail, is still there as the longest gaps.

bet: can several pieces be read in together
change: before building it: does apple's matrix kernel give a row the same bits whatever the row count? multiplied 656 rows at once and compared the first 1, 3, 66, 164 and 400 rows against the same rows run alone, for four decoder matrix shapes.
result: at 66, 164 and 400 rows every value is bit-identical to the 656-row run. at 1 and 3 rows almost every value differs, by up to 1.5e-05: the kernel takes another path for very few rows.
why: the engine only uses this kernel from 32 rows up, so reading several pieces in together would not change a row's bits, as long as the switch between the two paths sits below 32. that boundary is not yet located, and the batched prefill itself is not built.

bet: find where apple's matrix kernel changes paths
change: multiplied 1,664 and 6,400 rows at once and compared every row count from 1 to 80, plus 85 to 96, 104, 208, 800, 1,600 and 3,200, run alone from row 0 and from row 37, for all ten matrix shapes the prefill and encoder use.
result: past a boundary every value is bit-identical to the big run, from either start row and up to 6,400 rows. the boundary grows with the inner width: 10 rows at 1,024 and 2,048, 30 at 6,144, 40 at 4,096, 90 at 4,320 (the conv front) and 75 at 7,680 (the projection out of it). below it almost every value differs.
why: it settles the open question in the last line: decoder pieces of 32 rows or more (where the engine already uses this kernel) can share matrix products bit-safely. it also showed the encoder's last conv group, at 13 rows per chunk, fell below the 75-row boundary whenever it held 5 chunks or fewer.

bet: the encoder's bits depended on the conv group size
change: the projection out of the conv front ran once per group of chunks, so the last group's row count (and kernel path) depended on the group, which is derived from device memory. it now runs once over every chunk of the clip; the three convolutions keep their groups, at 208 rows per chunk or more, past their boundary.
result: harness: groups of 1, 3, 4 and 8 chunks give 0 differing values on the short (48 tokens) and long (1,515 tokens) clips. the medium and long clips' encoder bits change (their last group held 4 and 5 chunks), the short clip's do not. probe: tokens and candidates the same on all three, margin short 0.02, medium 0.34 (was 0.36), long 0.05.
why: the encoder result is now a pure function of the clip on any device. costs one extra 48 mb buffer for a two-minute piece, counted in the scratch reserve.

bet: silent fallbacks to other rounding
change: gemm, rms norm and both attention paths used try? on their work buffers and either returned without encoding anything or, in gemm, fell back from apple's kernel to the bandwidth kernel. they now throw. which kernel runs is set only by the shape, the row count and a new per-call flag: a decoder step never uses apple's kernel, so a host allowed 32 rows or more no longer switched steps onto it. every tensor's shape and byte count is checked against config.json at load.
result: no speed change. step bits unchanged at the 12-row cap (the step path was already the bandwidth kernel below 32 rows). probe passes.
why: an allocation failure or an unusual batch width used to change bits silently. now it fails with a clear error or keeps the same kernel.

bet: cpu time between decoder steps
change: measured each step's wall time inside step() against the gpu's own clock for its command buffer, 281 greedy steps of three rows on the long clip and 11 on the short.
result: long: 52.0 ms wall, 51.1 ms gpu, gap 0.9 ms. short: 45.9 ms against 45.3 ms, gap 0.65 ms. in the per-kernel profile the layer matrices take 36.7 ms and the output head 7.6 ms of 52.6, attention 6.8 ms.
why: encoding about 400 dispatches and the weight lookups cost under 2% of a step, so caching weight references or encoding ahead cannot buy more than that. the step is gpu-bound.

bet: more weight loads in flight per thread
change: the three-row kernel with the loads of 2, 4 or 8 pairs of quads issued before their adds, same add order. microbenchmark of a whole step's matrices, interleaved, 8 rounds.
why: two pairs ahead is inside noise and more is slower, the compiler already pipelines the loads. the kernel is at about 86 gb/s, near what this access pattern gets on an m4.

bet: weights through threadgroup memory
change: 64 weight rows per threadgroup copy a 64 x 128 tile into threadgroup memory with neighbouring lanes reading neighbouring bytes, then each thread adds its own row from there.
result: slower at every width: 3 rows 65.7 against 50.1 ms, 12 rows 103.6 against 53.9. and not bit-identical to the plain kernel, though the adds are written in the same order.
why: the barriers cost more than coalescing saves. the bits changing with the same written order is a warning: the compiler's choice to fuse a multiply and add depends on the code around it.

bet: widen the next matrix while the last one multiplies
change: two and three 32-bit weight copies taking turns in the prefill, so a widen has no dependency on the multiply before it. medium clip, interleaved 1, 2, 3, 1 and 1, 2, 1, 2 buffers, 6 to 8 rounds, gpu clock.
result: 1 buffer 562 and 554 ms median, 2 buffers 552 and 563 ms. inside noise (another process was on the gpu).
why: within one command queue metal runs the widen kernel and apple's kernel one after the other anyway. overlap would need a second queue with events.

bet: read several pieces in one prefill
change: new engine call prefill(pieces:): every matrix product runs once over all pieces' rows, so each matrix is widened once and apple's kernel gets more rows, while attention and the output head run per piece. a piece below 32 rows is read alone first. the one-piece prefill now goes through the same code.
result: bit-identical to reading each piece alone, every cache value and logit: short, medium, medium, short; three mediums; long and short. gpu time, interleaved, 6 rounds (gpu shared with another process): short+medium+medium+short 1,728 to 1,053 ms median (-39%), three mediums 1,555 to 1,138 ms (-27%), long+short 3,069 to 2,905 ms (inside noise).
why: saves the widening and the small-batch matrix cost on every piece after the first. it pays when short pieces arrive together, as in many files at once. the scheduler does not call it yet.

bet: the host reads every waiting piece in one pass when nothing is running, using the engine's multi-piece prefill, so twelve medium clips at once finish sooner
change: admission takes a group of waiting pieces that fit the rows and the cache, encodes each, then makes one prefill call for the group. with pieces running it still takes one per step.
result: twelve medium clips at 12 rows, three interleaved rounds of two runs: old host 12.74, 12.20, 11.25, 11.08, 10.99, 10.97x realtime; group host 12.45, 12.02, 11.02, 10.66, 10.99, 10.93x. tokens and candidates the same on all three golden clips, margins 0.02, 0.34, 0.05.
why: no gain, inside thermal drift. only the first four pieces share a pass; after that pieces finish at different steps and are replaced one at a time, so the shared pass saves about 0.3 s once in an 11 s run. the engine call stays for a scheduler that refills in groups.

bet: where the first encode of a run spends its extra 0.4 s
change: timed load, a 1 s silent warm-up and short clips in one process, then split the first conv command buffer into encoding, gpu time and the wait between the kernel taking it and the gpu starting it.
result: load 0.13 s. the first command buffer of a run waits 0.57 to 0.97 s before the gpu starts it, encodes in 8 ms and runs in 4 to 10 ms: the driver mapping every page of the 4.08 gb weight buffer for the gpu, about 2.3 us a page. the app's 1 s warm-up already pays it: after warm-up a short clip encodes in 0.06 s and a medium in 0.11. after 20 to 40 s idle the first buffer waits again, 0.05 to 0.46 s.
why: a measurement, no code change. the cost is the weight mapping, not pipelines, scratch or matrix descriptors, and prepare() already moves it before the first piece.

bet: map the weight pages on the cpu first
change: at load, 4 or 8 threads read one byte of every page of the mapped checkpoint before the first command buffer.
result: the touch takes 0.25 s (4 threads) to 0.71 s (8), and the first command buffer still waits 0.66 to 0.77 s.
why: the gpu's mapping is separate from the cpu's, so the touch only adds load time.

bet: a residency set for the weights
change: at load, one MTLResidencySet holding the weight buffers, requestResidency() and added to the queue, so the mapping is made once and kept while the engine lives. control, candidate, control, twice more control, candidate, control; each run loads, warms with 1 s of silence, then reads short, idles 20 s, short, idles 40 s, short.
result: bit-identical (probe: tokens and candidates the same, margins 0.02, 0.34, 0.05). requestResidency takes 0.77 to 0.92 s inside load, so load goes 0.13 to 0.9 to 1.1 s and warm-up drops 0.64 to 1.67 s to 0.34 to 0.69: load plus warm-up 1.20 to 1.85 s against 1.25 and 1.78, the same. after idling, the first buffer waits 0.054 to 0.081 s with the set and 0.046 to 0.456 s without (controls 0.144, 0.456, 0.109, 0.078, 0.364, 0.171, 0.083, 0.046). the gpu was shared with another process for part of it (short decode 0.55 to 1.4 s).
why: cold start only moves the cost into load, and after idle the last control (0.083, 0.046 s) matched the candidate, so it does not beat both neighbours. it would also keep 4 gb of file pages wired while the engine is loaded. worth a retry on a quiet machine with longer idles (minutes) if pieces after a pause feel slow.
